# Quantization

Also called: Value quantization, Precision reduction

## Overview
Quantization reduces the precision of volume data values to lower memory footprint and bandwidth requirements, enabling efficient storage and rendering of large datasets [S1][S2, unofficial]. It differs from its siblings, such as [Vector Quantization](907-vector-quantization.md) and [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md), by serving as the fundamental lossy step that maps continuous or high-precision data to a discrete set of indices, which are then often further processed by entropy coders or specific structural encoders [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
Not given in the sources.

## Subtopics

### [Attribute Quantization](1912-attribute-quantization.md)
Attribute quantization specializes in reducing the precision of voxel attributes, primarily colors and normals, to lower memory footprint while maintaining perceptual quality. It differs from [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md) and [Uniform Quantization](5855-uniform-quantization.md) by using perceptually uniform color spaces (CIELAB) and geometric mappings (Octahedron Normal Vectors) rather than generic linear mappings. Choose this method when rendering detailed scenes with millions of distinct attribute values where human perception limits can be leveraged to discard insignificant variations.

### [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md)
Scalar quantization (per-block) is a random-access decompression method that reconstructs voxel values on-the-fly from compressed data by mapping a block of voxels to a local range defined by block-specific minimum and maximum values. It differs from general scalar quantization by computing range parameters locally per block rather than globally, and from hardware-accelerated block-coding by relying on software-defined linear interpolation formulas. Choose this method when parallel GPU decompression is required without loading full-resolution data into memory.

### [Uniform Quantization](5855-uniform-quantization.md)
Uniform quantization maps a continuous range of source data values to a discrete set of integer indices using equal spacing between levels. It differs from its siblings, such as [Non-uniform Quantization](5858-non-uniform-quantization.md), by allocating quantization levels with constant step size regardless of the data distribution. Choose this method for simple bit-depth reduction (e.g., 32-bit float to 8-bit integer) when the data has a narrow dynamic range or uniform distribution.

### [Chroma Subsampling](6512-chroma-subsampling.md)
Chroma subsampling reduces the bitrate of volumetric data by lowering the resolution of chrominance components (U, V) while maintaining the luminance component (Y) at full resolution. Unlike direct subsampling, this method defines one color value for every eight adjacent corners, preserving color quality at low bitrates. It is distinct from sibling methods because it specifically targets perceptual redundancy in color channels, preventing the "grey object" artifact common in non-subsampled low-bitrate encoding. Choose this method when color fidelity is secondary to luminance detail and bitrate is constrained.

### [Differentiable Quantization for Neural Fields](10195-differentiable-quantization-for-neural-fields.md)
Differentiable quantization reduces the memory footprint of neural radiance fields by compressing grid values to single bytes during the optimization process, preventing quality degradation associated with post-training quantization. Unlike standard scalar or uniform quantization, this method integrates quantization into the training loop using a straight-through estimator, ensuring the model adapts to the low-precision representation. Choose this method when training neural implicit representations where post-training quantization would cause significant quality loss.

### [Neural Implicit Network Compression](10414-neural-implicit-network-compression.md)
Neural Implicit Network Compression (INR) replaces explicit grid storage with a coordinate-based neural network that maps spatial coordinates directly to field values, serving as simultaneously compressed storage and a queryable data source. Unlike traditional lossy compressors, INRs allow direct evaluation at arbitrary resolutions. The primary distinction from sibling methods like [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md) is the replacement of discrete lookup tables with continuous function approximation, enabling infinite resolution at the cost of significant training overhead and non-interactive inference speeds in early implementations. Choose this method when infinite resolution is required and interactive rendering speed is not the primary constraint.

### Lossy Quantization for Coarsened Patches
Lossy compression for coarsened patches in the bintree hierarchy. Quantization error $q$ is proportional to coarsening error $c$: $q = qc$, where $q$ is a fixed constant usually $< 1$. A single unified error is recomputed and nested for each patch. Quantization levels are restricted to power-of-two multiples of vertical resolution $\Delta z$ for efficient bit-shift implementation. Shift $k$ is calculated as: $k = \lceil \log_2(\epsilon_q / \Delta z) \rceil + 1$ if $\epsilon_q \ge \Delta z$, else $0$. All finest level vertices have zero shift. Vertices classified as boundary (corners $C$, legs $L$, hypotenuse $H$) and interior $I$. Corners stored at full precision. Quantization of original height values (not residuals) ensures adjacent patches agree on shared boundaries [S1].

### HSV Colour Sorting
A technique to preserve colour quality during DXT1 compression by reordering colours based on HSV values [S2, unofficial]. The effectiveness of HSV sorting depends on which component (H, S, or V) is the most frequent in the voxel data’s set of colours [S2, unofficial].

### Interpolation Symmetry Quantization
A method to improve the accuracy of quantized weights by exploiting the symmetry of linear interpolation between segments [S3]. Quantize both $w$ and $1 - w$ using the codebook generated by the scalar quantizer. Keep the representation resulting in the lower error. Store either $(i, j, w)$ or $(j, i, 1 - w)$ in the output stream. Linear interpolation: $(1 - w)s_i + w s_j$, where $(i, j, w)$ is equivalent to $(j, i, 1 - w)$ [S3].

### Position Lattice Quantization
An attempted method to compress Gaussian positions by quantizing them to a lattice structure and embedding positional constraints into the training process [S4]. Fails to compress positions without introducing significant rendering error [S4]. Identified as a future research direction for end-to-end positional compression [S4].

### Quantization and Entropy Encoding/Decoding Pipeline
The compression procedure involving quantization followed by entropy encoding (range-coder) for compression, and entropy decoding for decompression [S5]. Convert compressed data to non-negative values to enable compression into int8 format, then revert to original range during decompression. Formula: $\hat{x} = \frac{D(E(Q(q \cdot x) - Q(q \cdot \min(x)))) + Q(q \cdot \min(x))}{q}$, where $E$ is entropy encoder, $D$ is entropy decoder, $Q$ is quantization, and $q$ is the quantization parameter [S5]. $q$: The quantization parameter. Data is multiplied by $q$ to expand the data range, enhancing quantization precision. Adjusting $q$ trades off reconstruction quality and model storage size [S5].

## Background
Quantization is a fundamental technique in data compression, widely used in volume rendering to manage the high memory bandwidth and storage requirements of large volumetric datasets. In the context of volume rendering, it is often applied to scalar fields, attribute fields (colors, normals), and neural network weights. The technique has evolved from simple uniform quantization to more sophisticated perceptual and differentiable methods tailored for specific rendering pipelines and neural representations.
